claims.text: Oxidation resistance and material integrity in multiprincipal-element alloys are governed by which elements preferentially oxidize and whether they form a continuous protective scale.
Cr and Al are examples of the alloying elements with the highest oxygen affinity.
Selective oxidation of Cr or Al produces adherent, slow-growing chromia or alumina scales.
Continuous chromia or alumina scales block oxygen ingress and preserve the bulk alloy.
Mn is the major oxide-forming element during high-temperature oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi.
Mn oxidation in CrMnFeCoNi produces non-protective oxides.
Mn-rich oxides are easily spalled.
Mn-dominated oxidation depletes the bulk CrMnFeCoNi alloy of Mn.
Nanoscale chemical ordering, grain-boundary segregation, or other local chemical heterogeneity mediates which elements dominate the oxide scale and stabilizes protective oxide formation.
Controlling relative elemental diffusion and oxidation kinetics can enhance oxidation resistance.
Equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi is a homogeneous, single-solid-solution alloy in the proposed initial state.
Reducing Mn and/or increasing Cr or Al will bias oxidation toward formation of a protective scale.
Processing that promotes nanoscale chemical ordering will bias the surface composition toward protective-oxide-forming elements.
At elevated temperatures, constituent elements have different diffusion rates and oxygen affinities.
Mn-dominated non-protective oxidation causes rapid degradation of the baseline alloy's material integrity.
The modified alloy will have a lower oxidation rate and reduced oxidation-related mass gain than the baseline.
The modified alloy will maintain or improve its mechanical integrity after prolonged high-temperature exposure.
The proposed governing behavior should hold in air from approximately 750 to 1300 degrees Celsius.
The hypothesis may not apply in non-oxidative environments or where molten-salt corrosion and other mechanisms dominate.
The proposed controlled test compares baseline and modified samples after isothermal oxidation at 800 degrees Celsius in air for 100 hours.
